concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: immersive technology
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

Digital heritage preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve heritage, whether cultural, educational, scientific, ecological, or other, and it involves archiving, digitizing, and using immersive technologies such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR).

In digital heritage preservation, immersive technologies can recreate a physical space as a virtual world, such as a virtual tour, and, if properly designed, allow users to interact with entities in the virtual world, making the experience more engaging than accessing information through a computer screen.

Virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies permit a global audience to explore heritage sites, artifacts, and intangible aspects of culture remotely from home without visiting the physical site.

The use of virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies in heritage preservation is known to play a pivotal role in promoting the preservation of heritage for the benefit of future generations.

concepts.name: metaverse
concepts.definition: The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.

defining_facts.text: The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.

The metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology, while one broad view is that it reimagines the way humans interact with the digital world.

In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction with digital content, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions with occasional three-dimensional interaction.

The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software.

concepts.name: immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

defining_facts.text: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.

Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.
In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.
Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.
